who: The over-leveraged long on the perp itself, whose position is closed for them by Binance's liquidation engine as an IOC market order into whatever bids exist
why_they_keep_paying: Leverage is the only reason to hold a perpetual instead of spot, so the venue's economics — 20x-125x access, tiered maintenance margin, a clearance fee on every liquidated position, an insurance fund and ADL sized for the flush — are all built on the assumption that the leveraged long base rebuilds after each one, and measured open interest does rebuild within weeks of every cascade. The individual does not choose to pay: once mark price crosses maintenance margin the exchange sells at whatever the book offers, in size, at a moment they cannot decline, and BitMEX-based measurement puts daily forced liquidation at 3.51 % of outstanding longs versus 1.89 % of shorts at an average 60x leverage, so the long side is both the larger and the more frequent payer.
what_would_end_it: A hard cut in accessible leverage (the July 2021 move from 100x/125x to 20x is the historical precedent, and a further cut to ~5x would remove most of the fuel), or a liquidation design that stops routing the flush through the public book — full pre-emptive partial liquidation on tiny margin deficits, an auction/backstop-vault model that absorbs the position off-book at bankruptcy price, or portfolio/cross-collateral margin deep enough that maintenance breaches become rare. Sustained loss of the retail leveraged base to spot ETFs or jurisdictional bans would shrink it without changing the mechanism.
notes: The payer is real; the claim about the payment's form and timescale is where it breaks. (1) The payment is not one thing. It splits into a Liquidation Clearance Fee charged on notional that goes to Binance and its insurance fund — the exchange, not any trader, collects this — and a liquidity premium paid to whoever holds a resting bid at the instant the IOC order arrives. Binance's own protocol document describes 'one large Immediate or Cancel order (IOCO) to offload the position into the market', with the remainder becoming a Bankrupt Position that the insurance fund takes over at bankruptcy price, i.e. off-book. Only the middle slice is available to an external buyer, and it is available for the seconds the IOC order is live. The Hyperliquid HLP evidence is the cleanest read on who actually collects it: a co-located backstop vault sitting on the bid, earning ~$41.5m in a weekend. That is a latency business, not a patience business. (2) The horizon does not match the object. The claim asserts that 'a 10 percent drawdown inside 7 days is a cascade'. It is not. Cascades in the documented events repriced in minutes; the arXiv study of seven Binance USDⓈ-M BTCUSDT cascades works on 1-minute bars and finds no event-invariant signature at all — early-warning signals live in price for endogenous-buildup crashes and vanish or relocate to leverage variables for exogenous shocks. A multi-day drawdown on an hourly clock is a regime, and most 10 %/7-day drawdowns on these symbols contain no forced-selling event worth naming; conversely the real flushes are over long before the next hourly bar closes. A gate at that resolution selects on 'price fell', not on 'someone was forced to sell'. The claim's own framing concedes this when it calls the 20 %/30-day arm a regime, but it then treats both arms as expressions of the same payer. They are not the same payer. (3) The mechanism is not stationary across 2019-2024, which matters for a pooled backtest over that window. Accessible leverage fell from 125x/100x to 20x in July 2021 and to 20x for new accounts for 60 days; mark price is an index over a basket of spot exchanges rather than the perp's own last trade, so a perp-book-only wick cannot trigger the next liquidation and the reflexive loop the claim describes is deliberately damped; Smart Liquidation attempts partial reduction before full liquidation, so events are incremental rather than whole-position dumps; and the insurance fund grew large enough that ADL is rare. Every one of those changes shrinks the concession reaching the public book. A payer measured on 2019-2020 BitMEX-era data (the 3.51 %/60x figures) is not the payer of 2023. (4) The public record of this payment on Binance is structurally unmeasurable. Since April 2021 the liquidation order stream pushes only the single largest order per symbol per 1000 ms; Bybit and OKX cap their feeds similarly. In exactly the bursts that constitute a cascade, published liquidation totals are a small and unknown fraction of the truth, so no dataset the project can obtain will let it verify that a given drawdown was forced selling rather than ordinary selling. (5) The mechanism is symmetric and the claim only uses half of it. The same design liquidates crowded shorts on the way up — the leveraged bear in H0006 is the same party viewed from the other side — so 'forced seller with no choice about timing' is not evidence of a directional edge for a buyer; it is evidence that the venue converts leverage into two-sided overshoot. (6) The counterparty framing is loose in one further respect. The liquidated long's loss is transferred to whoever is on the other side of the perp position, which is predominantly the profitable perp short and the maker who filled them, not a buyer who arrives afterwards at a lower price. A later buyer receives a better entry price, which is a different thing from receiving the liquidated long's money. (7) The structural pedigree is sound and independent of Binance: this is the margin spiral of Brunnermeier-Pedersen, and it appears with the same signature on BitMEX, OKX, Bybit, dYdX and Hyperliquid, in DeFi lending liquidation bonuses, and in TradFi fire sales. So the answer to the question asked is yes, with high confidence, and the honest qualifier is that the party paying is durable while the channel through which a scheduled hourly-clock depositor could receive it is not established.
